summary: This unit teaches you to find, read and use the written information behind every fabrication job: standards, specifications, welding procedures, drawings, machine manuals, consumable data sheets and safety data sheets. You will learn to find what you need quickly, understand the words, units, abbreviations, tables and symbols, and apply the information correctly when you set up, weld, maintain and check. You will also learn what to do when information is missing, out of date or contradictory.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). A welder works from documents as much as from skill: the drawing says what to make, the specification says what standard it must meet, the welding procedure says how to weld it, the machine manual says how to set up and look after the machine, and the data sheets say how to use the consumables and chemicals safely. This unit teaches you to **read those documents correctly and act on them**.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who must set up equipment or carry out work from written instructions.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Tell a standard, a code, a specification, a WPS, a drawing, a manual, a data sheet and a safety data sheet apart, and say what each is for.
Use the contents page, index, glossary, appendix, section numbers and on-screen search; check the document matches the machine or job.
Read "shall", "should" and "may" correctly, and the signal words and symbols of safety information.
Convert between metric and imperial units, and read section sizes, drawing abbreviations and welding symbols.
Read tables, charts and rating plates
Find a setting in a table, read a machine's rating plate and work out what a duty cycle allows.
Set up a machine, choose a setting, follow maintenance and fault-finding instructions, and record what you did.
Use only the current issue; stop and ask when documents disagree or something is unclear; look after the documents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on kinds of documents, finding information, tables, units, abbreviations, drawings, specifications, the wording of standards, safety information, welding symbols, labels and data sheets, maintenance and fault-finding.
A **written paper** with short answers (abbreviations, conversions, names of documents and parts) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: using a machine manual and a consumable data sheet to set up a welding machine for a job, and interpreting a fabrication drawing and specification, then marking out and checking a part. You write down the page where you found each fact.

blocks.note: When you use a document in a practical, note the page or section number beside each fact. It shows the assessor where the fact came from, and lets you find it again.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Document
Who writes it
What it tells you
rows: A national or international standards body, such as the Bureau of Standards Jamaica (BSJ), ISO, the American Welding Society (AWS) or the British and European bodies (BS EN)
Agreed rules for how work or products must be made, tested, described or qualified: for example the rules for welding symbols, for testing welders, or for steel grades
A standards body; made compulsory by law or by a contract
A standard that must be followed for a type of work, such as a structural welding code or a building code
The designer, engineer or customer, for one job or product
What the finished work must be: material and grade, sizes and tolerances, process, weld sizes, preheat, finish and inspection
The company, often tested and approved
How to make a particular weld: process, consumable, size, current or settings, polarity, joint preparation, position, preheat
Shapes, sizes, tolerances, material, joints and welds, and how parts fit together
How to install, set up, use and care for the machine safely
Checks, maintenance schedule, fault-finding and repair, often for trained technicians
Every part, often on an exploded drawing, with its part number for ordering
Classification, sizes, current or voltage ranges, polarity, positions, storage and re-drying
The maker or supplier of a chemical product
Hazards, safe handling and storage, PPE, first aid, fire-fighting, spills and disposal
What job is to be done, how many, for whom and by when

blocks.p: Standards are written so that work done in different places, by different people, comes out the same and is safe. A **specification** usually names the standards the job must meet, and a **WPS** turns them into instructions a welder can follow at the bench.

blocks.note: The **Bureau of Standards Jamaica (BSJ)** is the national body that publishes Jamaican standards and adopts international ones. In Jamaican workshops you will also meet American (AWS), international (ISO) and British and European (BS EN) standards, and manuals written for American or European machines. Read the document's front pages to see which standard it follows.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Knowing that you have the right document

ul: For a manual: the **model number** (and, where it matters, the serial number) on the cover matches the machine's rating plate.
For a drawing or specification: the **job number, title and revision** match the job card, and it is the latest issue.
For a data sheet or label: the **classification and size** match what the drawing or WPS asks for.
For an SDS: it is for the exact product in your hand, from its supplier.

blocks.p: Manuals and standards are long. You do not read them from the start: you go straight to the part you need, then read that part fully.

head: Part of a manual
Where
What it is for
rows: Model, title, issue or revision and date
Chapters and sections **in order**, with page numbers: use it when you know which chapter the topic belongs to
General warnings that apply to every task
Supply needed, output range, duty cycle, size and weight
Connecting the supply and leads, what each control does, how to set up and use the machine
The maintenance schedule and the fault-finding table
Part numbers on an exploded drawing; the electrical circuit, for technicians
Special words and what they mean
Topics in **alphabetical order** with page numbers: use it when you know the word but not the chapter

flow: Check that the manual matches the machine (model number) and is the latest issue
Decide exactly what you need to find, for example how to change the polarity
Look in the contents for the right chapter; if it is not obvious, look in the index
Try other words for the same thing: "polarity", "output terminals", "connections", "leads"
On a screen copy, use the search tool (for example Ctrl+F)
Read the whole step, its diagram and every warning box before you start
Use the glossary for new words and the appendix for extra tables; follow cross-references such as "see 6.2"
If it is still unclear, ask your instructor or supervisor rather than guess

ul: Section numbers like **5.3.2** mean chapter 5, section 3, part 2. They make it easy to tell someone else exactly where a fact is.
Figures and tables are numbered too ("Figure 4", "Table 2"); the text refers to them by number.
Many makers put the manual online; a QR code on the machine may link to it. Make sure an online copy is for your exact model.

sections.title: The language of standards and safety

blocks.p: Standards and specifications choose these words with care. Reading them wrongly can make work fail inspection or be unsafe.

head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: A requirement: it has to be done. Work that does not do it does not meet the standard.
"Electrodes shall be stored in a holding oven after the packet is opened."
A recommendation: good practice, expected unless there is a good, agreed reason not to
"The work clamp should be placed close to the joint."
"Run-off plates may be used at the ends of the joint."
Possibility or ability, not an instruction

blocks.p: Labels and manuals use **signal words** to show how serious a hazard is. Read the whole message, whatever the word.

head: Signal word
Meaning
Example
rows: The most serious: death or serious injury **will** happen if it is ignored
"DANGER: high voltage inside. Do not remove the cover."
"WARNING: electric shock can kill. Do not touch live parts."
Minor or moderate injury could happen
"CAUTION: hot surface. Allow to cool before handling."
Damage to the equipment or property, not injury
"NOTICE: do not block the air vents, or the machine will overheat."

blocks.note: A warning box such as "Disconnect from the mains before removing the side panel" is an instruction to switch off **and** unplug or isolate first, every time, even for a quick look.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Chemical labels and safety data sheets use standard pictograms: a black symbol in a **red-bordered diamond** (the GHS system).

head: Pictogram
Hazard
Workshop example
rows: Thinners, acetone, solvent degreaser, anti-spatter aerosol, paint
Oxygen; some pool and cleaning chemicals
Argon, CO₂, oxygen and acetylene cylinders
Corrosion (liquid eating a hand and metal)
Burns skin and eyes; attacks metal
Pickling paste for stainless steel, some rust removers
Toxic: can kill in small amounts
Harmful or irritant: skin or eye irritation, drowsiness
Health hazard (person with a star on the chest)
Serious long-term harm, such as cancer or lung damage
Some paints and solvents: never pour down a drain

blocks.p: Every SDS has the same **16 sections** in the same order, so you always know where to look.

head: Section
Heading
What you find there
rows: Product name, supplier, emergency phone number
What to do for contact with eyes or skin, breathing it in, or swallowing it
Which extinguisher to use; hazards in a fire
Safe use; storage temperature; keeping away from heat and sparks
Ventilation and the PPE: gloves, goggles, respirator
Flash point and other data; what it reacts with; health effects
Effects on the environment; how to get rid of it and its container

blocks.note: Read the SDS **before** you first use a product: the hazards (2), handling and storage (7) and PPE (8), and know where the first aid (4) is. Some solvents give off poisonous gases when their vapour meets an arc or hot metal, so check whether a product may be used near welding.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Jamaica uses metric units. Sizes on engineering drawings are in **millimetres** unless the drawing says otherwise, often with one note: "All dimensions in mm".
1 m = 1000 mm; 1 cm = 10 mm. Pressure is given in **bar** or **kilopascals (kPa)**: 1 bar = 100 kPa. Temperature is in **degrees Celsius (°C)**.
Always write the unit beside a number. "Set 15" could mean 15 A, 15 V or 15 L/min.

blocks.p: Older drawings, American machines and gauges, and imported data sheets use imperial units. Check which way you are converting: multiply to go one way, divide to go back.

head: To change
Do this
Worked example
rows: Cubic feet per hour (cfh) to litres per minute (L/min)

blocks.note: A converted size is rarely exactly a metric stock size. If a ¼ in plate is called for, 6 mm plate is close but thinner. Ask the supervisor which to use before you cut; never just round and hope.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Steel sections are written in a set order. The usual pattern is the outside sizes first, then the thickness, all in millimetres.

head: Written as
Means
rows: Square hollow section, 40 mm by 40 mm, 3 mm wall
Rectangular hollow section, 100 mm by 50 mm, 5 mm wall
Circular hollow section (round tube), 48.3 mm outside diameter, 3.2 mm wall
Equal angle, both legs 50 mm, 5 mm thick
Parallel flange channel, universal beam, universal column (heavier structural sections)

blocks.h: Reading drawings: scale, views and lines

head: Feature
What to know
rows: Drawing size : real size. At 1:10, a line 32 mm long on the drawing is 320 mm in real life. Work from the written dimensions, not by measuring the print.
Front elevation (seen from the front), **plan** (seen from directly above) and end elevation (seen from the end)
Hidden edges that cannot be seen from that side
Thin chain line (long and short dashes)
Centre lines of holes and round parts
A detail drawing shows one part with all its sizes; an **assembly** (general arrangement, GA) drawing shows how all the parts fit together

head: Abbreviation
Meaning
rows: Pitch circle diameter: the circle on which a ring of hole centres lies, as in "6 holes on 100 PCD"
Centres: the distance between the centres of holes or parts
Typical: the same size applies to all similar features
Not to scale: do not measure the drawing
Across flats: the size of a nut or bolt head, and of the spanner that fits it
Revision: the version of a drawing or document
Manual metal arc (stick) welding; ISO process number 111
Gas metal arc welding with a wire; MAG with solid wire is ISO process 135
Flux-cored arc welding; ISO process 136 with gas
Tungsten inert gas welding; ISO process 141
DC electrode positive / DC electrode negative

sections.title: Reading tables, charts and rating plates

blocks.p: Find the **row** for your case, then move across to the **column** for the value you need. Read the headings and units first, and any footnotes.

In this example table, a 3.2 mm electrode is set between 90 A and 130 A. Start near the middle (about 110 A), make a test bead on scrap, and fine-tune. Many tables say the range is for the flat position: use the lower part of it for vertical and overhead.

blocks.note: Every maker's figures are different: use the table on **your** packet or data sheet, not one from memory or from a different brand.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Take a packet of **E7018** electrodes. Check every item before you weld:

head: On the packet
What it tells you
rows: Classification E7018 (and often an ISO code too)
E: an arc welding electrode. 70: weld metal of at least 70 000 psi tensile strength. 1: all positions. 8: a low-hydrogen coating and the current it uses. It must match the drawing or WPS.
Diameter and length, for example 3.2 × 350 mm
The size the job or WPS asks for
The range for each diameter: start near the middle and fine-tune on scrap
Current type and polarity, for example AC or DC+ (DCEP)
How to set the machine and connect the leads
The welding positions it may be used in
How to keep it dry; the holding oven and re-drying temperatures and times
Lets the consumable be traced if a weld is ever questioned: record it where the job needs it

blocks.p: The **rating plate** (data plate) on a welding machine gives its model, serial number, supply and output ratings. A typical inverter's plate might read:

head: Marking
Meaning
Example
rows: Supply voltage, number of phases and frequency
Largest and effective current drawn from the supply: used to size the supply circuit
**Open-circuit voltage**: between electrode and work when the machine is on but not welding
Welding (output) current at each duty cycle
Conventional load voltage at that current
How well the case keeps out solid objects and water: higher numbers are better

blocks.p: The **duty cycle** is the percentage of a **10-minute** period that the machine can weld at a given current without overheating. The rest of the 10 minutes it must cool, switched on so its fan runs. The higher the current, the lower the duty cycle.

ul: Welding beyond the duty cycle overheats the machine. Most machines have a **thermal cut-out** that stops the output and lights a warning lamp until they cool; repeated overheating shortens the machine's life and can cause damage or a fire.
Duty cycles are measured at a set air temperature (often 40 °C). In a hot workshop, or with the machine in the sun or its vents blocked, it will cut out sooner.

blocks.p: MIG machines and wire data sheets often give a chart of wire speed and voltage for each plate thickness and wire size. Treat these figures as a **starting point**: set them, make a test weld on scrap of the same thickness and position, and fine-tune. Record the settings that worked.
A specification for a fabricated item might say:

ul: **Material:** MS plate 10 THK and RHS 100 × 50 × 5, to the grade named.
**Process and consumable:** MMAW (111), E7018, 3.2 mm, kept in a holding oven after opening.
**Welds:** fillet welds 8 mm leg minimum, both sides, unless shown otherwise.
**Preheat:** a minimum temperature, for example 100 °C, where the plate is thick.
**Inspection:** 100% visual inspection; faults repaired before painting.
**Finish:** remove spatter and sharp edges; one coat of primer and two of paint.

head: Wording
What it means in practice
rows: At least this. "6 mm leg minimum": 6 mm or more passes; 5.5 mm fails.
No more than this. "Gap 3 mm max": 3 mm or less passes.
The tolerance: "500 ± 2" means anything from 498 to 502 mm passes.
The steel around the joint must be heated to at least 100 °C before welding, and checked with a temperature crayon or thermometer, as the procedure says
Each side of the joint must meet the size, not just the average

blocks.p: A WPS gives the welder the exact recipe for a weld: process, base metal, joint design and preparation, position, consumable type and size, current range and polarity (or wire speed and voltage, gas and flow rate), preheat, and cleaning between runs. Follow it as written. If you cannot meet it (wrong consumable in the store, wrong machine), stop and tell the supervisor.
A **welding symbol** on a drawing tells the welder what weld to make and where. Its parts:

head: Part
Meaning
rows: Points to the joint to be welded; the side it touches is the **arrow side**
The horizontal line joined to the arrow; the weld symbol sits on it
The type of weld: a **triangle** is a fillet weld; a **V** is a V-groove (butt) weld; two parallel lines a square butt weld; a V with one upright side a bevel
Beside the weld symbol, on the left: for example the fillet size
On the right: the length of each weld and, for intermittent welds, the distance between their centres
**Field (site) weld**: made on site, not in the shop
A fork at the end holding a note, such as the process or the WPS number

head: System
Arrow side
Other side
Fillet size
rows: The number is the leg length
Weld symbol on the **solid** reference line
Weld symbol on the **dashed** line drawn beside it
"a5" means a 5 mm throat; "z7" means a 7 mm leg

blocks.note: The two systems show the side differently, so check which one the drawing uses (its notes or title block usually say). If you are not sure which side to weld, or what a size means, ask before you weld.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Using manuals for set-up, maintenance and fault-finding

blocks.h: Setting up a machine from its manual

flow: Check the manual matches the machine; read the safety chapter
Check the supply on the rating plate (voltage, phase, current) matches the outlet and its breaker
Read the duty cycle for the current you will use
Find the polarity for your consumable on its packet, and how to connect the leads in the manual
Switch off and isolate the machine before connecting or swapping any lead
Set the controls as the manual and data sheet say
Make a test weld on scrap and fine-tune
Record the settings and any problems

blocks.note: If the manual says the machine needs a 220 V supply and the outlet is 110 V, or the breaker is smaller than the manual asks for, do not plug it in. Report it so that a qualified electrician provides the right supply. Never change plugs or wiring yourself.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **maintenance schedule** lists the checks and jobs to be done, and how often. For example:

head: How often
Typical tasks (follow your machine's manual)
Who
rows: Check cables, plug, holder or torch, work clamp and gas hoses for damage; check connections are tight
Clean the wire feed rolls; check the contact tip and nozzle; clean spatter from the torch
Blow out dust from inside the machine; check internal connections
A qualified person, with the machine unplugged

ul: Follow the schedule even when the machine seems fine: it stops faults before they happen.
Use the parts and methods the manual gives. Do only the tasks you are trained and allowed to do.
Record each job in the **maintenance log**: what was done, the date and your name.

blocks.p: A **troubleshooting** or fault-finding table has three columns: **problem**, **possible cause** and **remedy**. Find your problem, then check the causes in the order given, starting with the simplest and safest.

head: Problem
Possible cause
Remedy
rows: Wrong roll groove for the wire
Set the pressure as the manual says
Wire tangles at the drive rolls (birdnesting)
Liner blocked or tip burnt back
Leave it switched on to cool; clear the vents; weld in shorter spells

blocks.note: If a fault needs the case opened or anything electrical, it is for a technician. Switch off, isolate, tag the machine DO NOT USE and report it.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Applying information: issues, conflicts and records

blocks.p: Documents are revised when a customer changes a size, a better method is found or a safety problem is corrected. Each issue has a **revision** letter or number and a date. An old issue can give the wrong size, material or setting, or miss a new warning.

ul: Check the revision and date against the list of current documents, or with the supervisor, before you start.
Do not work from an old photocopy, a marked-up copy from another job, or a photo on a phone, unless the supervisor confirms it is current.
When a new issue arrives, old copies are removed or clearly marked as superseded.

blocks.h: When documents disagree or something is unclear

flow: Stop: do not guess and do not pick the answer you like
Check that you have the latest issue of each document
Write down exactly what disagrees or is unclear, with the page or section
Show the supervisor both documents and ask
Wait for a clear answer before going on with that part
Record the answer on the job card, with the date and who gave it

head: Situation
What to do
rows: The specification asks for E7018 but the store has only E6013
Tell the supervisor before welding and wait for a decision; never swap consumables or write the wrong one on the record
The drawing shows a 6 mm weld and the job card says 8 mm
Stop and ask which is right; record the answer
The manual for your model is missing
Ask for the correct manual or the maker's online copy; do not use one for a different model
A word or symbol is new to you
Check the glossary or legend, then ask

blocks.p: After using a document to set up or check something, record the information that matters: the settings used, the consumable and its batch number, checks made and results, problems found, and your name and the date. Records let anyone see later how the job was done, and they are often required by the specification.

ul: Keep manuals, drawings and data sheets clean, dry and in their set place, so anyone can find them when needed.
Keep papers away from sparks, hot metal, oil and water while you work: use a clear folder or holder.
Return them when you finish. Never tear pages out or write on controlled copies.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can say what a standard, code, specification, WPS, drawing, manual, parts list, data sheet and SDS are for.
I can check that a document matches the machine or job and is the current issue.
I can find information using the contents, index, glossary, appendix, section numbers and search.
I can explain shall, should, may and can.
I can explain the signal words DANGER, WARNING, CAUTION and NOTICE, and the common hazard pictograms.
I can find the right section of a safety data sheet and act on it.
I can convert inches, feet, psi, °F, pounds and cfh to metric units and back.
I can read section sizes and common abbreviations on drawings and lists.
I can read a current table, a rating plate and a duty cycle, and use a settings chart as a starting point.
I can read a specification's requirements, including minimum, maximum, tolerance and preheat.
I can read a simple welding symbol: arrow, reference line, weld type, size, all round, field weld and tail.
I can set up a machine from its manual, follow its maintenance schedule and use its fault-finding table.
I can stop and ask when documents disagree, record what I did and look after the documents.

terms: A section at the back of a document with extra tables, charts and diagrams
A standard that must be followed, by law or by contract
The list of chapters and sections, in order, with page numbers
The percentage of 10 minutes a machine can weld at a given current
A weld made on site; shown by a flag on the welding symbol
A list of special words and their meanings
An alphabetical list of topics with page numbers, at the back
A record of the maintenance done, with dates and names
A list or drawing of a machine's parts with their part numbers
The plate on a machine giving its model, serial number, supply and output ratings
The version of a drawing or document, shown by a letter or number
Safety data sheet: 16 sections of safety facts about a chemical product
DANGER, WARNING, CAUTION or NOTICE, showing how serious a hazard is
A document saying what a particular job or product must be and meet
Agreed rules for how work or products must be made, tested or described
The amount a size may vary and still be accepted
A table of problems, possible causes and remedies
The drawing sign telling the welder what weld to make and where
Welding procedure specification: the recipe for making a weld

c1.title: A new welding inverter in Hayes
c1.text: Sanjay, a trainee at a workshop in Hayes, Clarendon, is helping to set up a new MMAW inverter. Its rating plate reads: U1 220 V 1~ 50/60 Hz; I1max 32 A; U0 70 V; X 30% / 60% / 100%; I2 200 A / 145 A / 115 A; IP23S. The manual's contents list: 1 Safety; 2 Technical data; 3 Installation; 4 Controls and operation; 5 Maintenance; 6 Troubleshooting; 7 Parts list; Appendix A Wiring diagram; Index. Section 3 says: "The machine shall be connected to a 220 V supply protected by a 32 A circuit breaker." The outlet Sanjay was shown is 220 V, on a 20 A breaker.

c2.title: A trailer drawbar in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Kimani is to weld a trailer drawbar at a shop in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. The specification says: "Material: RHS 100 × 50 × 5 and 10 mm MS plate. Process: 111. Electrodes: E7018, 3.2 mm; electrodes shall be kept in a holding oven after opening. Fillet welds: 8 mm leg minimum, both sides. Run-off plates may be used. Drawing TD-04 Rev C applies." The drawing in the job folder is TD-04 Rev B.

c3.title: An imperial drawing for a winch post in Port Royal
c3.text: A fishing co-operative in Port Royal, Kingston, wants a new winch post made from an old American drawing. The post is 2 ft 6 in tall, welded to a base plate 5/16 in thick, with four holes of Ø ⅝ in. At the post's foot, the welding symbol has a triangle below the reference line with ¼ beside it on the left, a circle and a flag where the arrow meets the line, and SMAW in the tail.

c4.title: A degreaser's safety data sheet in Discovery Bay
c4.text: A shop in Discovery Bay, St Ann, has bought a new solvent degreaser for cleaning parts before welding and painting. Its SDS shows the signal word DANGER, with a flame pictogram and an exclamation-mark pictogram, and says "Highly flammable liquid and vapour. Causes skin irritation." Akeem, a trainee, has been asked to read the SDS before the product is used.

c5.title: Looking after a MIG machine in Kingston
c5.text: Tyrone, a trainee at a fabrication shop in Kingston, is responsible this month for the shop's MIG machine. The manual's schedule says: daily, check the cables, torch and gas hose; weekly, clean the wire feed rolls and check the contact tip; every three months, a qualified person cleans the inside of the machine. Its fault table, for "wire feeds unevenly", lists in order: drive roll pressure wrong; wrong roll groove; liner worn or blocked; contact tip worn.

questions.q: Sanjay needs the part number for a new work clamp. Where in the manual should he look?
questions.why: The parts list gives every part, often on an exploded drawing, with its part number for ordering. Technical data gives ratings, and the wiring diagram is for technicians.

questions.q: At 200 A, how long must the machine rest in each 10 minutes?
questions.why: A 30% duty cycle at 200 A means 3 minutes of welding in every 10, so it must cool, switched on, for the other 7 minutes.

questions.q: What does "U0 70 V" on the plate tell Sanjay?
o: The voltage across the arc while it is burning steadily
The supply voltage the machine needs
The voltage at the holder when on but not welding
The highest voltage of the welding arc at 200 A
questions.why: U0 is the open-circuit voltage: present between electrode and work whenever the machine is on, even when you are not welding. It is why the holder is always treated as live.

questions.q: The manual says the supply "shall" have a 32 A breaker, but the outlet is on 20 A. What should Sanjay do?
o: Use the outlet, as both are 220 V
Use the outlet at low current only
Report it and wait for a suitable supply
Fit a 32 A breaker in the shop's panel himself
questions.why: "Shall" is a requirement. The outlet does not meet it, and the breaker may trip or the circuit overheat. A qualified electrician must provide the right supply; trainees never change wiring.

questions.q: Kimani's fillet weld measures 9 mm on one leg and 7 mm on the other. What is the result?
o: It passes, as the average is 8 mm
It fails, as one leg is under 8 mm
It passes, as one leg is over 8 mm
It fails, as 9 mm is too big a leg
questions.why: "8 mm leg minimum, both sides" means every leg must be 8 mm or more. A 7 mm leg is undersize; a 9 mm leg is acceptable because the size is a minimum.

questions.q: What does "Process: 111" in the specification mean?
questions.why: ISO process numbers are used in specifications and welding symbols: 111 is MMAW, 135 MAG with solid wire, 136 flux-cored, 141 TIG and 311 oxy-acetylene welding.

questions.q: What does "Run-off plates may be used" allow Kimani to do?
o: He must fit run-off plates at every joint
He is allowed to use them, but need not
He must never use them on this drawbar
He may use them only with written consent
questions.why: "May" gives permission without making it a requirement. "Shall" would make them compulsory.

questions.q: The specification calls for Rev C, but the folder holds Rev B. What should Kimani do?
o: Get Rev C from the supervisor before he starts work
Work from Rev B, as it is the copy he has been given
Work from Rev B and check the job against Rev C later
Mix the two, using whichever sizes look most sensible
questions.why: The specification names Rev C, and Rev B may have different sizes or welds. Work only from the current issue; the supervisor provides it and old copies are removed.

questions.q: How tall is the post in millimetres?
questions.why: 2 ft 6 in is 30 inches, and 30 × 25.4 = 762 mm. 610 mm is only the 2 feet.

questions.q: Which metric plate is closest to the 5/16 in base plate?
questions.why: 5/16 in = 0.3125 × 25.4 = 7.94 mm, so 8 mm is closest. The supervisor still confirms the substitute before the plate is cut.

questions.q: Which drill size is the nearest metric match for the Ø ⅝ in holes?
questions.why: ⅝ in = 0.625 × 25.4 = 15.9 mm, so a 16 mm drill is the nearest match. Check the size with the supervisor if a bolt must fit closely.

questions.q: What does the welding symbol at the post's foot ask for?
o: A ¼ in butt weld on the far side, made in the workshop
A ¼ in fillet weld on one side only, ground flush
Four ¼ in spot welds, one at each side of the post
A ¼ in fillet weld all round the post, made on site
questions.why: The triangle is a fillet weld and ¼ is its size (about 6 mm); on this American-style symbol, below the line means the arrow side. The circle means all round, the flag means a field (site) weld, and the tail names the process, SMAW (MMAW).

questions.q: Which SDS section tells Akeem which gloves and eye protection to wear?
questions.why: Section 8 gives the ventilation and the PPE to use. Every SDS has the same 16 sections in the same order, so the PPE is always in section 8.

questions.q: A litre of degreaser spills on the floor. Which SDS section tells the shop how to deal with it?
questions.why: Section 6 covers spills and leaks: how to contain and clean them up and what PPE to wear. With a flammable liquid, sources of ignition are removed first.

questions.q: What does the exclamation-mark pictogram on the degreaser warn of?
o: It irritates the skin or is harmful
It can explode if it is dropped or knocked
It burns the skin and eats into metal
It is a gas stored under high pressure
questions.why: The exclamation mark shows a lower-level health hazard such as skin or eye irritation. The flame pictogram warns that it catches fire easily.

questions.q: The wire starts to feed unevenly. Using the fault table, what should Tyrone check first?
o: The contact tip in the torch
questions.why: The table lists causes in order, simplest first. Drive roll pressure is quick and safe to check; internal work is for a qualified person.

questions.q: The three-monthly clean of the inside of the machine is due, and Tyrone is not a qualified person. What should he do?
o: Unplug it and blow the dust out of it by himself
Skip it, as the machine is still working
Tell the supervisor so a qualified person does it
Clean only the parts inside that he can easily reach
questions.why: The manual says a qualified person does it. Tyrone does only the tasks he is trained and allowed to do, and makes sure the job is not missed.

questions.q: After cleaning the feed rolls each week, what else should Tyrone do?
o: Write it in the maintenance log, dated and signed
Tell the next class verbally at the end of the day
Nothing, as cleaning the rolls is the whole job
Write the date on the machine's case in marker
questions.why: The maintenance log shows what was done, when and by whom, so nothing is missed or done twice and the machine's history is known.

questions.q: A label on a grinder says: "NOTICE: Do not block the air vents." What does the signal word NOTICE tell you?
o: Death will happen if it is ignored
It is advice that you may ignore
questions.why: NOTICE is used for damage to equipment or property, not personal injury. DANGER, WARNING and CAUTION are for hazards to people, from most to least serious.
